name: Ivan Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ivan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm at Holloway & Grant, a thirty-person accounting firm, and most of our clients are charities, housing co-ops and small social enterprises. A normal day is year-end accounts and a couple of tax returns, plus a lot of chasing people for receipts. I use an AI assistant all day: it drafts the notes to the accounts, matches bank lines and writes the first pass of my emails.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment a set of accounts finally balances and I can explain to a food bank's treasurer, in plain words, where their money went. What wears me out is the January rush on personal tax returns, when I'm doing eleven-hour days. My partner Dani teaches maths at a secondary school, and she says I talk about deadlines in my sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit, because the tools I use are good but not magic. I'd post that AI is a decent junior at an accounting firm, not a partner, and it still makes silly mistakes. At work I'd keep telling people to use it for the boring stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my job stays and I keep my nice pay. I've got over a year of costs saved and a small index fund, so I'd be fine. The part of me that likes new things would be a little disappointed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on doing what I do and keep sharpening how I use the tools. I'd build a proper checklist for the bank matching so the juniors stop trusting it blindly. I might take the charity reporting course I keep putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Comfortable, mostly. A bit flat, like a film that promised a twist and didn't deliver one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your work that worries you even if AI stays small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The charities are squeezed, so a few might stop paying us and go to a cheaper online firm. Our fees haven't gone up in two years. That's a firm problem more than a me problem, though, because there are plenty of firms hiring around here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Dani over dinner if this turned out to be the world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the robots aren't coming for my spreadsheets after all, so we can stop doom-scrolling. Then I'd probably still check the AI news every morning, because I can't help it.

say: The AI tools I use are a **decent junior**, not a replacement for a qualified accountant.
Everyone at the firm should use AI for the **boring work** and check what it produces.
think: My **job and pay** stay safe, and I've got more than a year saved.
The curious part of me would be **slightly disappointed** that nothing big happened.
do: Write a **checklist** so juniors stop trusting the AI's bank matching blindly.
Take the **charity reporting course** I keep putting off, probably in spring.
feel: **Comfortable** and secure, with a slight sense of **anticlimax**.
S0.quote: AI is a decent junior at an accounting firm, not a partner, and it still makes silly mistakes.
fieldNote: Ivan's **strong savings** and plentiful local jobs make him relaxed when AI stays small.
His main pre-existing worry is **squeezed charity clients**, but he sees it as the firm's problem.
He sounds almost **disappointed**, which fits someone who uses AI tools every day.

steps.text: Keep preparing year-end accounts for charity and co-op clients
Write a checking list for the AI bank-matching tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is our chance to stop doing data entry and start giving real advice. Online I'd say the savings shouldn't all go to partners and shareholders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means the firm hires fewer juniors and expects me to do the work of two people with software. My job's probably safe because I'm the one who knows the tools. But the ladder below me gets sawn off, and I worry about who trains the next lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to run the firm's AI rollout, so I'm the person they can't lose. I'd join the professional body's working group on AI and push for rules on checking AI-made accounts. And I'd start a short course in data analysis this year, about £1,200, which I can pay myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Busy and a bit uneasy. Excited about the work, but not about what happens to the trainees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two trainees, Kofi and Hannah, who do the bank reconciliations and the first drafts of tax returns. That's exactly what the software does now. I'd fight to keep them and move them onto client calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be pushing the AI rollout and also worrying about trainees losing work. How do those sit together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncomfortably. I'd rather be the one shaping it, with the trainees in the room, than leave it to a partner who just sees a cost line. If I sit out the AI rollout, it happens anyway and nobody at the firm speaks up for our trainees.

say: This is a chance to swap **data entry** for real advice to clients.
The **savings** from AI shouldn't all go to partners and shareholders.
think: My **job is safe** because I know the tools better than most people there.
The firm will hire **fewer juniors**, and nobody's thinking about who trains the next generation.
do: Volunteer to lead the firm's **AI rollout** so I shape how it's used.
Join the professional body's **working group** pushing for rules on checking AI accounts.
Start a **data analysis course** this year, costing about £1,200 from savings.
feel: **Uneasy** about what happens to the trainees below me.
S1.quote: If I sit out the AI rollout, it happens anyway and nobody at the firm speaks up for our trainees.
fieldNote: Ivan expects his **own job** to survive and grow, so his unease is about others.
His **progressive outlook** shows in who he worries about: trainees, not partners.
He'd rather **shape** the change from inside than resist it, and says so frankly.

steps.text: Volunteer to lead the firm's AI rollout and checking rules
Join the accountancy body's working group on AI-made accounts
Pay £1,200 for an evening data analysis course this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that this needs a shorter working week and proper public support, fast. I'd post that if software can do a qualified accountant's job by 2028, the gains have to be shared or we're in real trouble. I'd say it loudly and probably lose a few followers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job is gone, or near enough. Preparing accounts and tax returns is all screen work, so it lands on the first date, not three years later. My savings buy me time, but they don't buy me a career when software does accounts and tax returns better than I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd move as much as I can into savings and stop the index fund top-ups so I have cash. I'd go to every meeting the union and the professional body run and back any policy for income support. Then I'd look hard at work with people in it, maybe training as a maths teacher like Dani, because classrooms are hands-on and have a few more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. I like being the person who's ahead with new tools, and in this picture being ahead doesn't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Dani talk about that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether her job is safe longer than mine, and I think it is. Teaching is face to face with thirty teenagers, and robots that good are three years behind the AI. We'd probably decide she's the steady earner for a while, which is a strange flip for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday to Lisbon we've booked for next summer, and my gym membership. We rent, so I'd hold off on any idea of buying a flat. I'd keep the money liquid until I know what I'm doing.

say: This needs a **shorter working week** and proper public support, fast.
If software replaces **qualified accountants** by 2028, the gains must be shared.
think: Preparing accounts is all **screen work**, so my job goes on the first date.
My **savings** buy me time, but not a new career.
do: Stop **index fund** top-ups and hold more cash from the first month.
Attend **union meetings** and back any policy for income support.
Look into **teacher training**, because classroom work keeps going a few more years.
feel: **Frightened**, because being ahead on AI tools no longer protects him.
S2.quote: My savings buy me time, but they don't buy me a career when software does accounts and tax returns better than I do.
fieldNote: Ivan expects to **lose his job** on the first date because his work is all thinking work.
He sees Dani's **teaching job** as safer, since hands-on classroom work has three extra years.
His public line is **political**, while his private view is plain fear about his own career.

steps.text: Pause index fund top-ups and hold savings in cash
Attend union and accountancy body meetings on AI job losses
Back campaigns for a shorter working week and income support
Look into training as a secondary school maths teacher

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them, and I'd push for a proper retraining fund paid for by the firms that save money. At work I'd say we should be honest with the trainees now, not in 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is enough to land somewhere, if I start straight away. My job still ends, but I'd be 32, not 29, with more saved and a plan. Like I said with the fast one, the accounts work goes first because it's all thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend year one finishing the data course and then trying a part-time teaching qualification, so I've got two doors. I'd save an extra £400 a month into a separate account. And I'd write to our local MP about a retraining fund, with a few colleagues signing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but steadier. There's time to make a plan, and I like having a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the last year before 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By then I'd want to have taught at least some classes, maybe as a part-time tutor. I'd keep doing accounts until the firm stopped needing me, because the pay helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your job ends either way. Why does five years feel so different from two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I can switch on my own terms instead of being pushed. Two years of warning is a fire drill. Five years is a career change I get to choose.

say: We've got **five years**, so firms that save money should fund **retraining**.
We should be **honest with trainees** now, not in 2030.
think: Five years is **enough time** to land somewhere new if I start straight away.
My **accounting job** still ends, but I'd be older, richer and better prepared.
do: Finish the **data course**, then start a part-time **teaching qualification**.
Save an extra **£400 a month** in a separate account.
Write to the **local MP** with colleagues about a retraining fund.
feel: **Anxious** about the loss, but **steadier** because there's time to plan.
S3.quote: Two years of warning is a fire drill. Five years is a career change I get to choose.
fieldNote: The extra time turns Ivan's fear into **planning**, though he still expects his job to end.
He wants **two exits**: data work and teaching, which is more hands-on.
His politics stay consistent: firms that gain should **pay for retraining**.

steps.text: Start a part-time secondary teaching qualification after the data course
Put an extra £400 a month into a separate savings account
Write to the local MP with colleagues about a retraining fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years of warning is a gift if we use it and a disaster if we waste it. I'd keep pushing for retraining money and for the trainees to be told the truth early. Online I'd be the annoying person posting reading lists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is a whole career stage. I'd probably get to partner-track level, earn more, save a lot, and then move before 2036. My worry is that people around me, especially at the firm, will relax and do nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing accounts and get really good at running AI tools for clients, because that's the next eight years of work. I'd start the teaching qualification slowly, maybe in year three. And I'd put more into the index fund, since I'd have time for it to grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A bit uneasy, like knowing the lease ends on a flat you love.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dani and I might actually buy a place in this version, since I'd have years of good pay left. We'd want something near her school, not near my office, because her job lasts longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you leave accounting earlier than you need to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw the firm stop hiring trainees altogether, I'd take that as the signal. That'd tell me the people at the top have stopped believing in the job.

say: Ten years is a **gift** if we use it and a **disaster** if we waste it.
Trainees deserve to hear **the truth early** about where the job is heading.
think: A decade is a **whole career stage**, with time to earn and save a lot.
My real worry is colleagues **relaxing** and doing nothing until it's too late.
do: Keep doing accounts and get expert at **running AI tools** for clients.
Start a **teaching qualification** around year three, alongside work.
Increase **index fund** contributions while there's time for growth.
feel: Mostly fine, with a quiet **unease** like a lease running out.
S4.quote: Ten years of warning is a gift if we use it and a disaster if we waste it.
fieldNote: With a decade, Ivan expects to **keep earning well** and leave on his own schedule.
He'd buy a home near Dani's school, because her **hands-on job** lasts longer.
His signal to leave would be the firm **stopping trainee hiring** altogether.

steps.text: Become the firm's go-to person for running AI on client accounts
Begin a part-time teaching qualification around year three
Raise monthly index fund contributions while there's time to grow
Buy a flat with Dani near her school

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because my whole job is thinking work and there'd be no time to switch on my own terms. What would help is a paid retraining fund and a shorter week, so our trainees Kofi and Hannah aren't just dropped. For me personally, a fast-track into teaching would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets the money. If AI does my job for a tenth of the cost, someone is pocketing the other nine-tenths, and that's the real question. I'd rather be part of deciding that than read about it afterwards.

headlineQuote: If AI does my job for a tenth of the cost, someone is pocketing the other nine-tenths, and that's the real question.
portrait: Ivan is a **27-year-old accountant** at a firm serving charities and co-ops, using AI tools every day.
He has **over a year saved**, rents with his partner Dani, a maths teacher, and has no children.
He stays calm if AI stalls, but expects to **lose his job** if AGI comes by 2028.
His **progressive politics** shape everything: he worries for trainees and asks who pockets the savings.
Given time, he plans a move into **teaching**, because classroom work lasts longer than screen work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his job is all thinking work and there's no time to switch.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid retraining fund** and a shorter week, so trainees aren't simply dropped.
A **fast-track route** into teaching for people leaving desk jobs.
